analysis.title: GS flow and positioning observations
key_insights: Asia equities fell again as the market absorbs Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia and the prospect of tighter US AI chip export controls (MATCH Act and RASA). The desk says lost chip export revenue could redirect supply into the US market, while economies reliant on US technology face weaker near-term capex and possibly slower long-term productivity growth. Asia's supply chain is described as particularly exposed.

Defensive rotation is extreme. Relative multiple expansion in defensives is approaching levels last seen decades ago. XLU has outperformed TLT by roughly 5 percentage points over 20 sessions (about 3 standard deviations over 20 days).
The desk argues equities are pricing a growth scare that the bond market has not acknowledged. If bonds are not going to rally, it asks why investors pay an immense premium for safety and quality.

Rates stayed subdued on Monday despite oil, stocks and growth all falling. Williams reiterated a cautious, hawkish-leaning stance that policy must stay sufficiently restrictive. Warsh gave a more balanced view of AI, acknowledging potential for an investment bust alongside the productivity upside.
The desk expects that if equities keep falling, the distribution of rate outcomes should shift quickly away from hikes, citing Warsh's history of focusing on financial conditions (FCI).

Recent IT disruptions across cloud infrastructure, commercial airlines and banks were not confirmed as malicious. The desk argues enterprise cybersecurity budgets are starting to behave like non-discretionary capex, with spending tilting toward automated threat detection, real-time telemetry and identity verification, and that more spending feels baked in for 2027-2030.

The desk flags robotics as a possible larger AI unlock in the physical world. GPU-accelerated simulation (NVIDIA Isaac Lab) and differentiable world models (SuperMimic, which compressed 100,000+ whole-body motions into three hours on a single GPU) have commoditized lower-level balance and locomotion.
Nvidia reports after the close on 11/18 (the note says tomorrow). The desk suspects near-term numbers could be robust, but says the market has no idea what multiple to apply to 2028 to 2030 earnings.

Equities are pricing a growth slowdown while rates and FX barely respond, so either equities are overreacting or rates and FX are underreacting. The recent NDX lows are the technical line in the sand: a hold lets a base form, a break risks another mechanical leg lower as CTAs sell and volatility rises.

US close: S&P 500 -192bps at 7,416 with a $5.3bn MOC to buy, NDX -267bps, Russell 2000 -175bps at 2,741, Dow -141bps at 51,608. VIX rose to 23.12, WTI fell to $85.39, US 10Y at 5.12%, gold 3,850, DXY 103.60, Bitcoin $64,959.
Volume was 17.916bn shares versus a YTD daily average of 18.555bn. The floor rated activity a 4 out of 10, with asset manager and hedge fund flows muted ahead of a busy week.

Tech and AI sold off on Jensen's departure and reports that Congress is moving to pass tighter AI chip export rules. Moves: NVDA -4.5%, DRAM -6%, SMH -5%, neoclouds -7%. The FT also reported Jensen is eyeing a possible comeback to Nvidia.

Staples saw a flight to safety, helped by reversion after the prior week's heavier short supply across nearly all subsectors per GS PB. Single-stock moves: TSCO +4%, BBWI -9%, VSXY -5%, ARMK +1% on EPS.
Upcoming catalysts: NKE investor day tomorrow, and earnings from AS, VIK and HD.

Derivatives: index options are expensive across the board. The S&P realized its entire weekly implied move in one session (QQQ and IWM close behind), causing a jump in vol and skew. Option volumes were muted after a week of light positioning and a rise in ETF short interest.
Desk flow in single stocks: buying of capped upside in AMZN, MU and TSM, and longer-dated outright downside protection in semis.
NVDA options imply a 7.8% one-day move for tomorrow. The S&P straddle for the rest of the week is 2%, which the desk says still looks underpriced in the current regime.
